title: Neonatal jaundice (hyperbilirubinaemia)
subject: paediatrics
setting: Postnatal ward, SNCU, NICU, outpatient follow-up
summary: For babies of 35 weeks or more, measure TcB or TSB in every newborn before discharge and urgently if jaundice appears in the first 24 hours. Plot by age in hours on the AAP 2022 curves for gestation and neurotoxicity risk factors to decide phototherapy, escalation of care (2 mg/dL below the exchange level) or exchange transfusion.

sections.title: Assess risk
items: Visual assessment is unreliable, especially in darker skin: look for jaundice at every check (at least every 12 hours before discharge) but decide with a bilirubin measurement.
Jaundice in the first 24 hours is pathological until proven otherwise: measure bilirubin urgently (NICE: within 2 hours) and look for haemolysis.

Neurotoxicity risk factors (use the lower treatment curves): gestation below 38 weeks, albumin below 3.0 g/dL, isoimmune haemolytic disease (positive DAT), G6PD deficiency or other haemolysis, sepsis, and significant clinical instability in the previous 24 hours.

Risk factors for significant hyperbilirubinaemia: lower gestation, jaundice before 24 hours, pre-discharge bilirubin close to the phototherapy threshold, haemolysis, and a sibling who needed phototherapy.
Other risk factors: exclusive breastfeeding with poor intake, cephalhaematoma or bruising, infant of a diabetic mother and Down syndrome. Screen for G6PD deficiency where it is common.

sections.title: Measure and investigate
items: Measure TcB or TSB in all newborns between 24 and 48 hours of age, or before discharge if earlier. Interpret by exact age in hours, not day of life.

TcB can be used at 35 weeks or more after 24 hours; confirm with TSB if TcB is at or within 3 mg/dL (51 micromol/L) of the phototherapy threshold or is 15 mg/dL (257 micromol/L) or more. Use TSB in the first 24 hours, below 35 weeks, and during or after phototherapy.
When phototherapy is needed: maternal and infant blood group and DAT, CBC with smear and reticulocyte count, G6PD, and albumin if near the escalation level; sepsis evaluation if the baby is unwell.
Do not subtract direct (conjugated) bilirubin from the total when making treatment decisions.

sections.title: Phototherapy
items: Babies 35 weeks or more: start phototherapy at or above the AAP 2022 hour-specific threshold for gestation, using the lower curve if any neurotoxicity risk factor is present. Babies below 35 weeks need lower, gestation-specific thresholds (NICE charts or unit protocol).
Give effective phototherapy: blue-green LED light (about 460 to 490 nm) at an irradiance of at least 30 microW/cm2/nm, maximal skin exposure, eye protection. Do not use sunlight.

Continue breastfeeding and support lactation; give expressed breast milk or formula only if intake is inadequate or the baby is dehydrated. Use IV fluids only if oral or enteral feeding is not possible.
Monitor with TSB during phototherapy, more often with haemolysis or when close to the escalation threshold.

Stop phototherapy when TSB has fallen at least 2 mg/dL (34 micromol/L) below the threshold at which it was started (NICE: 50 micromol/L below threshold). Check for rebound, sooner if there was haemolysis, prematurity or phototherapy in the first 48 hours (NICE: 12 to 18 hours after stopping).

sections.title: Escalation of care and exchange transfusion
items: Escalation of care begins when TSB reaches the exchange threshold minus 2 mg/dL: treat as an emergency, admit to NICU for intensive phototherapy, check TSB every 2 hours, send albumin, CBC, blood group, DAT and cross-match, and prepare for exchange.

Isoimmune haemolytic disease (Rh or ABO) with TSB at or above the escalation threshold: IVIG 0.5 to 1 g/kg IV over 2 hours, repeat after 12 hours if needed. NICE: 500 mg/kg over 4 hours if bilirubin rises by more than 8.5 micromol/L per hour despite intensified phototherapy.
Urgent double-volume exchange transfusion if TSB reaches the exchange threshold despite intensive phototherapy. Continue phototherapy during and after the exchange.
Exchange immediately, regardless of level, for any sign of acute bilirubin encephalopathy: hypertonia, arching, retrocollis, opisthotonos, high-pitched cry, fever or recurrent apnoea.

sections.title: Discharge, follow-up and prolonged jaundice
items: Plan follow-up by how close the pre-discharge bilirubin is to the phototherapy threshold and by age at discharge (AAP 2022 follow-up chart): the smaller the gap and the earlier the discharge, the sooner the repeat bilirubin and review.
Teach parents to seek review for deepening yellow colour, poor feeding, lethargy, pale stools or dark urine.

Jaundice beyond 2 weeks in formula-fed babies or 3 to 4 weeks in breastfed babies (NICE: beyond 14 days at 37 weeks or more, 21 days if preterm): measure total and conjugated bilirubin, ask about pale chalky stools and dark urine, and check CBC, blood group, DAT and newborn thyroid screening.
Conjugated bilirubin above 25 micromol/L (about 1.5 mg/dL) may mean serious liver disease such as biliary atresia: seek expert paediatric hepatology advice promptly.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Relying on visual estimation or day of life instead of hour-specific values.
Applying AAP 2022 curves (35 weeks or more) to preterm babies below 35 weeks.
Missing haemolysis (ABO, Rh, G6PD deficiency) in a rapidly rising bilirubin, or sepsis in an unwell jaundiced baby.
Using agar, albumin, phenobarbital (barbiturates), charcoal, cholestyramine, clofibrate or traditional remedies to treat jaundice; they are not recommended.

drugs.name: Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG)
drugs.dose: 0.5 to 1 g/kg IV over 2 hours; may repeat after 12 hours (AAP 2022)
drugs.notes: Isoimmune haemolytic disease with TSB at or above the escalation threshold. NICE: 500 mg/kg over 4 hours.

drugs.name: Phototherapy
drugs.dose: Irradiance at least 30 microW/cm2/nm, blue-green light 460 to 490 nm, maximal skin exposure
drugs.notes: Start at or above the hour-specific threshold; stop when TSB is at least 2 mg/dL below the starting threshold.
